content: Malawi has implemented a centralized system for patient monitoring, where teams conduct quarterly site visits to supervise and review data directly from patient cards. In contrast, South Africa employs a decentralized system, where individual facilities submit monthly and quarterly cohort data to the district level for validation and aggregation before forwarding it to provincial and national levels. If antiretroviral therapy (ART) registers are in use, cohort reports can be directly transcribed from these registers. Otherwise, an intermediary step is required, involving transcription from patient cards or folders into a register to aggregate the data. Aggregating cross-sectional reports manually can be labor-intensive and error-prone, especially when disaggregating data by age, sex, or specific indicators like the number of patients currently on ART. District health teams or supervisors must carefully validate this information by cross-referencing ART registers or, less routinely, patient cards. They should re-aggregate numbers, check for consistency over time, and compare data with reports from other health facilities when possible. Updated quarterly reports include indicators for HIV, TB/HIV, and HIV/MNCH, which require data from multiple registers. These indicators must be reported quarterly as mandated by national programs. Patient monitoring systems serve as a critical primary data source for quality assurance and improvement efforts. Health facilities already collect substantial data for routine patient monitoring, summarizing it in registers and logs, and reporting it to district and national levels. Leveraging this data to evaluate the quality of care provided to patients offers a valuable opportunity to identify and address gaps in the care cascade. Validating facility-level reports is essential once district health staff receive them. This can involve comparing current reports to past ones, checking for completeness, legibility, and unusual figures. Regular district meetings with each facility provide a platform to discuss data quality concerns or highlight exemplary data quality in validated reports. Electronic data verification is also crucial, as most electronic entries originate from paper forms. Before assessing data quality in electronic systems, it is necessary to validate the paper-based data sources. Electronic systems, while helpful, remain vulnerable to poor data quality, often at the point of data entry. Automated checks can be integrated into these systems to flag errors, such as blank fields, out-of-range numbers, or incorrect formats. However, even with these checks, data must be reviewed after entry and before aggregation to ensure high-quality registers or reports. Triangulation is a powerful technique for validating data by cross-verifying it from two or more sources. For example, the proportion of patients who received a viral load test or achieved viral suppression, as reported through the patient monitoring system, can be validated against laboratory data for the same period. Similarly, the number of individuals picking up medications from a pharmacy register can be compared with the number of patients on ART as recorded in the patient monitoring system. As chronic care services (e.g., HIV, TB) become integrated, triangulating data from different sources can enhance validation without increasing the data collection burden. This method can also be applied in case surveillance to verify data sources, including patient monitoring systems. The first step in improving the quality of HIV care is identifying processes that require enhancement. For instance, determining that laboratory equipment is broken occurs at the facility level, but replacing it is the district team's responsibility. If patients are not receiving necessary laboratory tests, the process can be improved by redesigning systems, such as clinic flow patterns, and testing these changes for effectiveness. Many countries have adopted national HIV indicators, which can also measure care quality. Additionally, patient chart or card abstraction can serve as a proxy for assessing health worker competence and practices in routine care settings. However, incomplete registers and patient charts or cards may pose challenges in some settings. The performance of healthcare providers is a critical predictor of care quality, although other confounding factors may also influence patient care. Patient charts or cards can provide clear information, such as adherence to national or global treatment guidelines or protocols, including prescribed antiretroviral regimens or the interpretation and use of laboratory results. Performance measurement reveals what is actually happening, as opposed to what is believed to be happening. It indicates whether tasks that should be performed are being done and done well. Even in small facilities where staff know patients well, performance measurement often uncovers surprising findings when data is compiled. Some indicators are required for district or national reporting, but facilities may choose to measure additional indicators based on their specific priorities. To define a sound indicator, it is necessary to establish the numerator (e.g., the number of patients from the denominator group who received a specific service) and the denominator (e.g., the group of patients eligible to receive the targeted service). If the data is not already collected as part of the standard patient monitoring system, steps must be taken to define how the data will be recorded, who will record it, and when it will be collected. Performance is measured over a specific time frame, and only patients actively seen during this period are included in the measured group. If the review is conducted annually, the time frame may be the last calendar year. However, for indicators requiring more immediate review, the time frame may be the last quarter. Depending on the assessment, only certain groups of patients may be eligible for inclusion in the review. For example, the indicator may apply to both men and women, children, or only specific clinical conditions. Other inclusion criteria could involve whether the patient is new or already on treatment. The list of eligible patients may also need to be sorted by age or gender, depending on the indicator's applicability. Ideally, all patients would be included when measuring an indicator (100% sample or census), but this may be labor-intensive without an electronic patient monitoring system. In settings with fewer patients, it may be simpler to review all charts. Alternatively, a sampling methodology can be used. For example, if there are 750 eligible patients for a specific indicator, and the sample size is determined to be 146, every fifth patient from an ordered list can be selected. The list must ensure that each patient is recorded only once. When a problem is identified, it is crucial to describe it in detail, specifying when, where, and with whom it occurred. Investigating the causes of the problem is essential, as different causes require different solutions. Solutions should address the root cause, be feasible, and not create additional problems. If multiple root causes exist, several solutions may be necessary. For example, if there is a lack of both equipment and training, solutions must address both issues. Data collected through patient monitoring systems can also inform supportive supervision visits by program managers, mentoring healthcare providers, and providing feedback for in-service training. Supportive supervision, clinical mentoring, and in-service training contribute to ensuring care quality. Regular district meetings with facilities should present a small number of indicators, compared across facilities and time. These indicators can be programmatic or for management purposes, depending on the need. Annual target-setting for district-level enrollment should be discussed, with enrollment targets set for each facility. Key programmatic indicators to monitor include the number of new and current patients on ART per facility per month, measured against district targets. Late ART initiation, defined as the proportion of patients starting ART with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³, should ideally decrease as patients are enrolled in HIV care and initiated on ART promptly upon HIV diagnosis. If the stages of the care cascade are adequately followed, this proportion should approach zero. If the proportion remains high, it is essential to investigate and address the underlying causes, such as poor linkage between HIV testing and care, drug stock-outs, or other systemic issues. Once improvements are made, the proportion should decrease over time. This indicator can be derived from ART cohort report forms, verified by reviewing ART registers and a sample of HIV patient cards if necessary. Tracking the final outcome status of HIV-exposed infants (HEI) at 18 months is critical. Following the HIV-infected mother and her HEI can be challenging in settings where antenatal care, postpartum care, and child health services are separate from HIV care and treatment. It is essential to ensure that the infant's HIV status is checked and that ART is initiated promptly if the infant is diagnosed with HIV.
